title: Wow! signal
summary: On a summer night in 1977 a radio telescope in Ohio heard something from deep space that looked exactly like a message. <mark>It lasted 72 seconds. In almost fifty years of searching, it has never come back.</mark>
coverCredit: Big Ear Radio Observatory and NAAPO, public domain

chapters.title: A search begins
chapters.summary: Big Ear had spent years mapping the radio sky.
chapters.body:
Big Ear had spent years mapping the radio sky. When that work ended, the money ended too. Rather than leave the telescope idle, the astronomers decided in 1973 to use it for something few others were doing: listening for signals from other civilisations.

The search was led by Robert Dixon and run almost entirely by volunteers. A computer recorded the sky around the clock, and people checked the printouts by hand.

It went on for more than twenty years, one of the longest searches of its kind.
chapters.marginNote: Run by volunteers.

media.title: Note
media.text:
An idle telescope,
put to a new use.

chapters.title: The night
chapters.place: Big Ear radio telescope, Delaware, Ohio
chapters.summary: Since 1973 Ohio State University's radio telescope, nicknamed Big Ear, had been searching the sky for signals from other civilisations.
chapters.body:
Since 1973 Ohio State University's radio telescope, nicknamed Big Ear, had been searching the sky for signals from other civilisations. Night after night it listened, and an IBM 1130 computer printed what it heard on long sheets of paper.

At 22:16 on 15 August 1977 the turning Earth swept Big Ear's view across a patch of sky in the constellation Sagittarius. For 72 seconds the computer recorded a signal that rose, peaked and faded away again. Nobody was in the control room. The numbers were simply printed with all the others.

A few days later Jerry Ehman, an astronomer who checked the printouts by hand, reached that sheet at his kitchen table. Among the usual columns of ones and twos, one column read 6, E, Q, U, J, 5. He circled it in red and wrote one word in the margin: Wow!
chapters.marginNote: Nobody was watching. The computer printed it anyway.

media.title: The printout
media.caption: The column Ehman circled, and his note in the margin.
media.credit: Big Ear Radio Observatory and NAAPO. Public domain.

chapters.title: The printout
chapters.summary: The printout follows a simple code.
chapters.body:
The printout follows a simple code. Big Ear split the radio band into 50 narrow channels, one column each. Every 12 seconds the computer printed one character per channel, telling how much stronger the signal was than the normal hiss of space.

A space meant weaker than the background. The numbers 1 to 9 meant that many times stronger. After that it switched to letters: A meant 10, B meant 11, and so on up to Z for 35.

Read that way, 6EQUJ5 is the shape of a hill: 6, 14, 26, 30, 19, 5. And it was in only one of the 50 channels. Natural sources spread their radio waves over many frequencies. A signal squeezed into one narrow channel looks much more like a transmitter.
chapters.marginNote: Play the tape: the six values turned into sound. Big Ear recorded numbers, not sound.

media.title: The six values of 6EQUJ5
media.caption: Each bar is one 12-second reading. The dotted curve is what a source fixed in the sky draws as the Earth turns it through the telescope's view.
media.credit: Chart drawn by AstPIE from the printed values.

media.caption: The original printout, with the column circled.

chapters.title: Ehman's circle
chapters.summary: Jerry Ehman was one of the volunteers.
chapters.body:
Jerry Ehman was one of the volunteers. A few days after the night of 15 August, he sat down with the latest stack of printouts, as he often did, and ran his eye down the columns of characters.

Most of it was ones, twos and spaces. Then, in one column, he saw 6EQUJ5. He circled it in red pen and wrote one word in the margin: Wow!

He showed it to Dixon and Kraus. They agreed it was the strongest and strangest signal they had ever recorded.
chapters.marginNote: A red pen and one word.

media.title: The circle
media.caption: Ehman's red circle and his word in the margin of the printout.
media.credit: Big Ear Radio Observatory and North American AstroPhysical Observatory. Public domain.

chapters.title: Kraus's telescope
chapters.summary: Big Ear was designed by John Kraus, a professor at Ohio State who had already invented a new kind of antenna, the helical antenna, still used on satellites today.
chapters.body:
Big Ear was designed by John Kraus, a professor at Ohio State who had already invented a new kind of antenna, the helical antenna, still used on satellites today.

Money was short. Much of the telescope was built by Kraus himself, his students and volunteers, working weekends for years, with help from the National Science Foundation.

When it was finished in 1961 it was one of the largest radio telescopes in the United States.
chapters.marginNote: Built at weekends.

media.title: Note
media.text:
Students, volunteers,
and five years of weekends.

chapters.title: The telescope
chapters.summary: Big Ear was not a dish.
chapters.body:
Big Ear was not a dish. A flat reflector more than 100 metres long tilted up or down and sent radio waves along an aluminium ground plane, as large as three football fields, to a fixed curved reflector that focused them onto the receivers.

It could not turn sideways. It let the Earth do the work: as the planet rotates, any point in the sky crosses its narrow view in about 72 seconds, exactly how long the Wow! signal lasted.

One detail is the most frustrating of all. Big Ear had two horns side by side, so a real source should pass through one and, three minutes later, the other. The signal appeared in only one. Big Ear was taken apart in 1998 to make room for a golf course.
chapters.marginNote: Two horns, three minutes apart. Seen in only one.

media.title: How Big Ear listened
media.caption: Radio waves hit the tilting flat reflector, travel along the ground plane to the fixed curved reflector and are focused back onto the two feed horns.

media.title: Note
media.text:
Horn 1: signal.
Horn 2, three minutes later: nothing.

chapters.title: The sky survey
chapters.summary: Before it listened for aliens, Big Ear made a map.
chapters.body:
Before it listened for aliens, Big Ear made a map. From 1965 to 1971 it swept the sky strip by strip as the Earth turned, recording every source of radio waves it could find.

The result, the Ohio Sky Survey, listed nearly 20 000 radio sources. Many had never been seen before: distant galaxies, quasars and clouds of gas.

Knowing the normal sky so well helped later. A new signal from a place where nothing was known stood out at once.
chapters.marginNote: First a map, then a search.

media.title: Note
media.text:
Know the normal sky,
and the strange stands out.

chapters.title: Big Ear's end
chapters.summary: Big Ear kept listening for another twenty years after the Wow!
chapters.body:
Big Ear kept listening for another twenty years after the Wow! signal, run mostly by volunteers. It was one of the longest searches of its kind.

The land it stood on belonged to Ohio Wesleyan University. In the 1980s the university sold it to developers, and in 1998 the telescope was taken apart to make room for a golf course.

Today a historical marker stands near the site. The printout with the red circle survives.
chapters.marginNote: The telescope is gone. The printout is not.

media.title: Jerry Ehman at Big Ear
media.caption: Jerry Ehman sitting on the structure of Big Ear, before the telescope was taken down.
media.credit: Big Ear Radio Observatory and North American AstroPhysical Observatory (bigear.org). Used here for the mockup only; permission needed before publishing.

chapters.title: Where it came from
chapters.summary: Because of the two horns, the signal has two possible positions, very close together, in Sagittarius, the Archer.
chapters.body:
Because of the two horns, the signal has two possible positions, very close together, in Sagittarius, the Archer. Its brightest stars look like a teapot, and the signal came from a little to the east of it, towards the crowded centre of our galaxy.

For decades no particular star could be linked to it. In 2022 the amateur astronomer Alberto Caballero searched the area for stars like our Sun and found one about 1 800 light-years away. So far, nothing has been heard from it.
chapters.marginNote: A reply would take 1 800 years to get there.

media.title: Note
media.text:
A Sun-like star nearby,
1 800 light-years off.
Silent so far.

media.title: Towards the centre of the galaxy
media.caption: The centre of the Milky Way rising over Rara, in Nepal. The signal came from this part of the sky.

chapters.title: Looking again
chapters.summary: If the signal came from a transmitter, it might send again.
chapters.body:
If the signal came from a transmitter, it might send again. Ehman and Dixon pointed Big Ear at the same strip of sky night after night.

They listened more than a hundred times over the following months. They heard nothing at all: not the signal, not anything like it.

A signal that appears only once is the hardest kind to study. Scientists cannot test it, measure it again or show it to anyone else.
chapters.marginNote: More than a hundred tries.

media.title: Note
media.text:
Once is not enough
for science.

chapters.title: The search
chapters.summary: If it came from a transmitter, it might come again.
chapters.body:
If it came from a transmitter, it might come again. Big Ear pointed at the same spot more than a hundred times. It heard nothing.

Robert Gray spent years on it, with a telescope at Harvard and then, in 1995 and 1996, with the Very Large Array in New Mexico, many times more sensitive than Big Ear. In 1999 he tried again from Tasmania. None of the searches found the signal, or anything like it.

In 2012 the Arecibo telescope in Puerto Rico even sent a reply towards Sagittarius. Today, large surveys scan the sky for narrow signals and find plenty. Almost all of them are satellites, aircraft or equipment on Earth.
chapters.marginNote: More than a hundred tries at Big Ear alone.

media.title: The Very Large Array
media.caption: Robert Gray used these dishes in 1995 and 1996 to search the spot for hours at a time.

media.title: Arecibo Observatory
media.caption: In 2012 this dish sent a reply towards Sagittarius, made of thousands of short messages from the public.
media.credit: H. Schweiker, WIYN and NOAO/AURA/NSF. CC BY 4.0

chapters.title: A reply in 2012
chapters.summary: On the 35th anniversary of the signal, the giant Arecibo radio telescope in Puerto Rico sent an answer.
chapters.body:
On the 35th anniversary of the signal, the giant Arecibo radio telescope in Puerto Rico sent an answer.

A television channel had invited people to write messages online. About ten thousand of them were beamed towards the Wow! signal's part of Sagittarius.

If anyone is there, at about 1 800 light-years, the reply will take about 1 800 years to arrive.
chapters.marginNote: Ten thousand messages, very slow post.

media.title: A reply to the Wow!
media.text: Messages from the public, sent from Arecibo.

chapters.title: The facts to explain
chapters.summary: Any explanation must fit a short list of facts, read from six characters and the way Big Ear worked.
chapters.body:
Any explanation must fit a short list of facts, read from six characters and the way Big Ear worked.

The signal was very narrow, in a single channel, close to the hydrogen frequency. It rose and fell over 72 seconds, exactly as a fixed point in the sky would as Big Ear's beam swept past it. It appeared in one horn and not in the other. And it was never heard again.

Something on the ground or moving fast through the sky would have looked different. That is why it is so hard to explain away.
chapters.marginNote: Four facts, no answer.

media.title: The rise and fall
media.caption: The six values of 6EQUJ5 against the shape a point in the sky would make.

rows: like a fixed point in the sky

chapters.title: The explanations
chapters.summary: Any explanation has to fit the same few facts: a narrow signal near the hydrogen frequency, a rise and fall that matched the turning sky, one horn instead of two, and silence ever since.
chapters.body:
Any explanation has to fit the same few facts: a narrow signal near the hydrogen frequency, a rise and fall that matched the turning sky, one horn instead of two, and silence ever since.

Four ideas are pinned to the board. Pick up a card to read what supports it and what speaks against it.

The hydrogen frequency is special. Hydrogen, the most common element, gives off a faint glow at 1420 megahertz everywhere in space. Astronomers use it to map the galaxy, so nobody on Earth is allowed to broadcast on it.
chapters.marginNote: Four ideas. Only one is still being tested.

explanations.title: A signal from another civilisation
explanations.proposedBy: The idea that made it famous, 1977
explanations.forText: It was very narrow, like a transmitter, close to the hydrogen frequency that others might choose because every scientist would know it. And it behaved exactly like a source fixed in the sky.
explanations.againstText: It never repeated, which a beacon meant to be found surely would. It carried no message or pattern, and it lasted only 72 seconds.
explanations.verdict: Nothing supports it beyond the signal itself.
explanations.imageCredit: The Arecibo message, sent by people in 1974. Arne Nordmann, CC BY-SA 3.0

explanations.title: Interference from the Earth
explanations.proposedBy: The first thing every astronomer checks
explanations.forText: Most unexpected signals are made by people: radar, aircraft, satellites. A reflection from space debris could in principle make a short spike.
explanations.againstText: Nothing on Earth should transmit at 1420 MHz. The 72-second rise and fall matched the turning sky, not something nearby. No satellite was in the right place.
explanations.verdict: It does not fit the shape or the frequency.

explanations.title: A passing comet
explanations.forText: Comets are surrounded by hydrogen, which glows at exactly this frequency. Two comets, undiscovered in 1977, were in that part of the sky.
explanations.againstText: Comets are far too faint to be seen so strongly. The comets were not in the right place, and the signal should have shown in both horns.
explanations.verdict: An interesting idea that did not survive the checks.
explanations.imageCredit: Comet Hale-Bopp, 1997. E. Kolmhofer, H. Raab, Johannes Kepler Observatory. CC BY-SA 3.0

explanations.title: A hydrogen cloud that flared
explanations.forText: Old Arecibo data show weaker signals of the same narrow shape from cold hydrogen clouds. A burst of energy, for example from a magnetar, could make one flare briefly and never in the same way again.
explanations.againstText: It needs a rare and very bright event at the right moment. The idea is new, other teams have not confirmed it, and no flare as strong as the Wow! has been seen.
explanations.verdict: The best natural explanation so far.

chapters.title: The comet idea
chapters.summary: In 2016 Antonio Paris, a teacher of astronomy, suggested that the signal came from a comet.
chapters.body:
In 2016 Antonio Paris, a teacher of astronomy, suggested that the signal came from a comet. Comets are wrapped in clouds of hydrogen, and two comets unknown in 1977 had been in that part of the sky.

The idea made headlines around the world. Other astronomers checked it quickly. The comets were not in the right place when the signal arrived, and their hydrogen glow would have been far too weak.

Most scientists rejected it. It was still a useful test: a clear idea that could be checked, and was.
chapters.marginNote: Checked, and rejected.

media.title: A comet
media.caption: Comet Hale-Bopp over Pennsylvania in 1997. Comets carry clouds of hydrogen around them.

chapters.title: A flare in the cold
chapters.summary: In 2024 Abel Méndez and his colleagues went through old recordings from the Arecibo telescope.
chapters.body:
In 2024 Abel Méndez and his colleagues went through old recordings from the Arecibo telescope. They found several faint signals at the hydrogen frequency that looked a little like the Wow!, only much weaker.

Their idea: a cold cloud of hydrogen gas, normally almost invisible, was suddenly lit up by a burst of energy from a distant star or dead star. For a short time the cloud would shine like a natural radio beacon.

It fits the narrow signal and the hydrogen frequency, and it would explain why nothing was heard again. It still has to be confirmed.
chapters.marginNote: A natural beacon, switched on briefly.

media.title: Note
media.text:
If it is right,
it will happen again,
somewhere.

chapters.title: Other strange signals
chapters.summary: The Wow!
chapters.body:
The Wow! signal is not the only time the sky seemed to be sending a message. The others show how a mystery usually ends: with a new kind of object in space, or with something ordinary on the ground.

In 1967 the student Jocelyn Bell Burnell found a pulse repeating every 1.34 seconds. Her team half-jokingly called it LGM-1, for Little Green Men. It was the first pulsar, a tiny spinning dead star.

For years the Parkes telescope in Australia picked up bursts that looked like they came from space, always during office hours. They came from the staff microwave oven, opened before it had finished.
chapters.marginNote: Most mysteries end in a new discovery, or a microwave oven.

media.text: The best candidate since the Wow!

chapters.title: Listening for others
chapters.summary: The idea of listening for other civilisations is older than Big Ear.
chapters.body:
The idea of listening for other civilisations is older than Big Ear. In 1959 two physicists suggested that the hydrogen frequency, the one the Wow! signal was near, would be the natural channel for anyone who wanted to be found.

In April 1960 a young astronomer, Frank Drake, pointed a 26-metre dish at Green Bank at two nearby stars like the Sun, Tau Ceti and Epsilon Eridani. He called it Project Ozma. For about 150 hours he listened, and heard nothing.

A year later he wrote the Drake equation, a list of the things you would need to know to estimate how many civilisations might be out there. Most of them are still unknown.
chapters.marginNote: The first time anyone listened on purpose.

media.title: The Ozma dish
media.caption: The 26-metre Howard E. Tatel telescope at Green Bank, used for Project Ozma in 1960.

chapters.title: The Drake equation
chapters.summary: In 1961 Frank Drake invited a small group of scientists to Green Bank to discuss the search for other civilisations.
chapters.body:
In 1961 Frank Drake invited a small group of scientists to Green Bank to discuss the search for other civilisations. To give the meeting an agenda, he wrote down an equation.

It multiplies together the things you would need to know: how many stars form, how many have planets, how many planets could support life, how often life becomes intelligent, how often it builds radio transmitters, and how long such civilisations last. The answer is how many might be sending signals in our galaxy right now.

We now know that most stars have planets. The other numbers are still guesses.
chapters.marginNote: An agenda, not an answer.

media.title: The Drake equation
media.caption: An illustration of the Drake equation and its factors.
media.credit: NOIRLab / AURA / NSF / P. Marenfeld. CC BY 4.0

chapters.title: Sending a message
chapters.summary: Listening is one half of the conversation.
chapters.body:
Listening is one half of the conversation. In 1974, to celebrate an upgrade of the Arecibo telescope, Frank Drake and his colleagues sent a message the other way.

It was 1 679 ones and zeros. Arranged in a grid of 73 rows of 23, they form a picture: numbers, the chemistry of DNA, a human figure, the Solar System and the telescope itself. It was aimed at a cluster of stars called M13, about 25 000 light-years away.

It was meant mostly as a demonstration. Any reply could not arrive for about 50 000 years.
chapters.marginNote: 1 679 bits, 25 000 light-years.

media.title: The Arecibo message
media.caption: The 1974 Arecibo message, with its parts coloured to make them easier to see.

media.title: M13
media.caption: The heart of M13, the star cluster the message was sent towards.
media.credit: ESA / Hubble and NASA. Public domain.

chapters.title: Listening today
chapters.place: Green Bank, Parkes and South Africa
chapters.summary: In 2015 a private foundation launched Breakthrough Listen, the largest search so far: ten years and about 100 million dollars to listen to a million nearby stars and a hundred nearby galaxies.
chapters.body:
In 2015 a private foundation launched Breakthrough Listen, the largest search so far: ten years and about 100 million dollars to listen to a million nearby stars and a hundred nearby galaxies.

It uses some of the biggest dishes in the world, including the Green Bank Telescope, the largest steerable dish on Earth, and Parkes in Australia. Unlike Big Ear, it records the whole signal, so a candidate can be studied again and again.

Its one strong candidate so far, from the direction of Proxima Centauri in 2019, turned out to be interference from equipment on the Earth.
chapters.marginNote: Recording everything this time.

media.title: The Green Bank Telescope
media.caption: The Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope, about 100 metres across, the largest fully steerable radio dish in the world.

chapters.title: What would solve it
chapters.summary: The Wow!
chapters.body:
The Wow! signal happened once, was recorded by an old computer in a simple code, and was only noticed days later. There is no way to measure it again. Every explanation has to fit six characters on a sheet of paper.

What would settle it is another signal like it, caught by modern equipment that records the full signal and can point several dishes at once. If a similar burst comes from a hydrogen cloud, the flare idea is confirmed. If a narrow signal ever repeats from the same star, with a pattern in it, it would be one of the biggest discoveries in history.

Until then it stays what it has been since 1977: the most famous question mark in radio astronomy.
chapters.marginNote: One more detection would change everything.

media.title: The Parkes telescope
media.caption: One of the dishes used today by surveys that look for narrow signals like the Wow!

media.text:
Status: still open.
Waiting for a second signal.

chapters.title: Why it still matters
chapters.summary: The Wow!
chapters.body:
The Wow! signal is not famous because it proves anything. It is famous because it is honest: a strong, clean signal, recorded carefully, that nobody has been able to explain.

It shows how science deals with something that happened only once. Every idea has to fit the evidence, every idea is tested, and "we do not know yet" is an acceptable answer.

Newer telescopes now record far more than Big Ear ever could. If anything like it happens again, it will not be missed.
chapters.marginNote: We do not know yet.

media.caption: The Allen Telescope Array in California, built to search for signals like the Wow!
